title: Building AI/BI Dashboards: Datasets, Pages and Widgets, Plus Notebook and SQL Editor Charts

concepts.heading: Datasets Feed Widgets
concepts.body: An AI/BI dashboard has two tabs. The Data tab holds datasets and the Canvas tab holds pages with widgets: visualizations, filters, text and images. A dataset is defined once, from a Unity Catalog table, view or metric view, or from your own SQL query, and any number of widgets on any page can read it. A table or view starts as a default `SELECT *` query that you can narrow. A dataset is a security decision as well as a layout one: viewers can reach all data in a dataset even when no chart shows a column, so Databricks recommends listing only the columns you need and adding a `WHERE` clause for the rows you need. A salary column that sits in the dataset is exposed even if every chart ignores it. Datasets travel with the dashboard when it is shared, imported or exported, so there is no separate query object to keep in step.

concepts.heading: Pages, Drafts and Publishing
concepts.body: A dashboard can hold several pages, which turns it into a multi-page report. A page can be cloned within the dashboard, and the datasets stay the same. A page copied into another draft dashboard brings its datasets as new, independent copies. Hide from published dashboard keeps a scratch page visible to authors only, which is safer than deleting it because deleting a page removes its widgets. New dashboards open as drafts; edits autosave but do not flow to a published version, and a draft can be shared only with users inside the workspace, who use their own credentials. Publishing creates a snapshot that stays unchanged until the next publish, so managers keep seeing the old numbers while you experiment. Discard changes restores the draft to the last published version. Opening a dashboard that was published before shows the published version first.

concepts.heading: Where Filtering and Aggregation Run
concepts.body: Dashboards avoid asking the warehouse again whenever they can. For small datasets, filtering and aggregation that come from filters or chart settings run in the browser after the first load, so they do not show up in query history. For large datasets they run on the backend, wrapped around the dataset query, and they appear in query history. This explains a common surprise: a filter on a small dataset reacts instantly, while the same filter on a very large dataset triggers a query. Query parameters always change the SQL itself, so they always run on the warehouse. The practical analyst rule is to shape the dataset first (needed columns, needed rows, pre-aggregated when the chart only needs totals), then let widgets slice it. Heavy transformations belong in the dataset query or in a view, not in many separate widgets.

concepts.heading: Charts in Notebooks and the SQL Editor
concepts.body: Outside dashboards you build a chart under a result: click + above the result and choose Visualization, then pick a type and fields. For bar, line, area, pie, heatmap and histogram charts you can aggregate in the visualization editor (sum, average, count and so on) instead of rewriting the query, and the aggregation covers the whole result, not only the rows the results table displays. A filter on the visualization also filters the results table, and the other way around, without changing the SQL. Clicking a legend entry hides or shows a series and double-clicking isolates one. A chart under a SQL cell offers Add to dashboard, which can create an AI/BI dashboard; charts from other languages and data profiles can only go to a notebook dashboard. Use the SQL editor or notebook for exploration and a dashboard for sharing a stable view.

examPoints: A question about viewers seeing columns no chart shows is testing that the whole dataset is visible to viewers, so the dataset query lists only needed columns and rows instead of `SELECT *`.
A question about hiding a working page, throwing away experiments, or what viewers see after edits is testing Hide from published dashboard, Discard changes, and the draft versus published snapshot.

A question about switching sum to average on a chart in the SQL editor is testing aggregation in the visualization editor, and one about sending a chart to a dashboard is testing that Add to dashboard exists only for SQL cells.

quiz.q: An analyst built a bar chart under a Python cell in a notebook and wants colleagues to see it on an AI/BI dashboard. What is the limitation she should expect?
choices: The chart can be added to a dashboard only when the notebook is attached to a serverless SQL warehouse instead of a general cluster
Only SQL cells offer Add to dashboard; other languages stay in a notebook dashboard
The chart is converted automatically, but its aggregation settings are dropped and must be rebuilt on the dashboard canvas
The chart is shared through Add to dashboard, which lists every dashboard the analyst may edit, whatever the cell language is
quiz.explain: Add to dashboard is offered for SQL cells. Charts and data profiles from other languages stay in a notebook dashboard, so the analyst would define a SQL dataset on an AI/BI dashboard and rebuild the chart there.

quiz.q: An author edits the draft of an already published dashboard, changing a filter and two charts. Managers open the dashboard the next morning and still see the old charts. What explains this?
choices: Draft edits sync to viewers only after the next scheduled refresh runs all the dataset queries again
Viewers always see the draft version when the author has CAN EDIT access, so the managers lack a needed permission
Autosave only covers widget layout, so changes to filters must be exported and imported to appear for viewers
Published dashboards are snapshots; draft edits wait for the next publish
quiz.explain: Draft changes autosave but do not sync with the published version. Viewers see the snapshot from the last publish, which is why authors can experiment safely and use Discard changes to go back.

recap: Define datasets once on the Data tab, select only the columns and rows viewers may see, and reuse them across pages. Drafts autosave privately and viewers see only the last published snapshot. Small datasets filter in the browser, large ones on the warehouse, and parameters always rerun the query. In the SQL editor and notebooks, aggregate in the visualization editor, and use Add to dashboard only from SQL cells.

title: Dashboard Parameters, Filters and Cross-Filtering, and Choosing the Right Visualization Type

concepts.heading: Parameters Change the Query
concepts.body: A parameter is a named marker such as `:start_date` in the SQL text; the value is substituted when the query runs. In the SQL editor you set the parameter's type (text, number, date and so on) in a widget, so colleagues type a value instead of editing SQL. In a dashboard dataset, parameters connect to filter widgets, or to a visualization as a static value set by the author so that several widgets on one dataset show different views. Always type the default value into the field under the parameter name and run the query, which saves the default. Because the value goes into the SQL, parameters filter before aggregation or inside a subquery, and they always rerun the query on the warehouse. Two patterns matter for the exam. Multiple selection requires `array_contains(:region, region)`, and enabling multiple selections is needed or the function raises an error. A range uses `:date_param.min` and `:date_param.max` with `BETWEEN`. Add `OR :param IS NULL` so that All returns every row.

concepts.heading: Field Filters or Parameters
concepts.body: A field filter narrows the dataset result by a column and needs no parameter in the SQL. Databricks recommends field filters for most interactivity: for small datasets they run in the browser without rerunning the query, and for large ones the filter is added to the query that the warehouse runs. They also support cascading, so choosing a region narrows the choices offered in a city filter. Use a parameter when the value must reach the query before a join, aggregation or subquery, or when you build a drop-down from a separate `SELECT DISTINCT` dataset and bind both the field and the parameter to the same filter widget. Filter scope has three levels. Global filters apply across all pages for widgets that share a dataset; page-level filters apply to one page; widget-level filters are fixed by the author and cannot be changed by viewers, so they give one chart a permanent slice. Date pickers, ranges, single and multiple value lists, text entry and range sliders are the available filter types, with some limited to fields.

concepts.heading: Cross-Filtering and Ignored Filters
concepts.body: Cross-filtering lets a viewer click a bar, a slice or a point in one chart to filter the other widgets built on the same dataset. The active filter bar at the top of the dashboard shows every global filter, page filter and cross-filter that is not set to All, so a viewer can see why numbers changed. When one chart must stay fixed while the rest of the dashboard reacts, the author sets that widget to ignore selected filters or cross-filter selections. That is different from a widget-level filter: an ignored filter exempts a widget from viewer choices, while a widget-level filter applies a permanent author-chosen condition. Filter values can also be set in the published dashboard URL, which is useful for bookmarked views. Cross-filtering depends on the shared dataset, so two charts on unrelated datasets will not respond to each other even if their column names match.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Right Visualization
concepts.body: Start from the question, then choose the type. A trend over time is a line chart, or an area chart when you also show how groups add up. Comparing categories is a bar chart. Shares of a total fit a pie, which is not meant for time series. The spread of one numeric column is a histogram, where the number of bins sets the grain, and a box chart compares quartiles across groups. Two numeric measures are a scatter chart, and a third measure as marker size makes it a bubble chart. Drop-off through ordered stages is a funnel with a step and a value column. A running total built from positive and negative steps, such as opening to closing balance, is a waterfall. A single headline KPI with a comparison value is a counter. A heatmap shows a number as colour across two categories and a pivot or table is for exact values. Custom Vega-Lite charts are still a Preview feature, so rely on built-in types.

examPoints: A question about letting viewers pick several values and also an All option is testing a multi-select parameter written with `array_contains` and an `OR :param IS NULL` branch, and a date range with `.min` and `.max`.

A question about a small dataset, a fixed chart slice, or one selection across pages is testing field filter versus parameter, widget-level versus page-level versus global filter, and ignored filters.

A question that describes the business need in words (trend, shares, drop-off, distribution, opening to closing balance, one KPI) is testing the type: line, pie, funnel, histogram, waterfall, counter.

quiz.q: A dashboard dataset has a few thousand rows, and viewers only need to narrow the chart by customer segment. A teammate proposes adding a query parameter for the segment. What does Databricks recommend instead?
choices: A field filter on the segment column, which small datasets apply in the browser without rerunning the query
A page of copies of each chart with the segment value typed into the dataset query by hand
A parameter bound to a text entry widget, so that every selection reruns the warehouse query before aggregation
A global parameter on the dataset that is hidden from viewers and set only by the author at publish time
quiz.explain: Field filters are the default recommendation: on small data they apply in the browser, on large data the filter is added to the query, and they cascade. Parameters are for values that must reach the SQL before a join, aggregation or subquery.

quiz.q: A finance analyst must explain how the opening cash balance of a quarter became the closing balance, with each inflow and each outflow as its own step. Which visualization fits?
choices: A stacked area chart with one series per inflow and outflow, plotted by week across the quarter
A funnel chart where every step is a cash category and the width shows the amount remaining
A waterfall chart where each category adds to or subtracts from the running total
A pie chart of the absolute value of each cash category, so executives see the share of each movement
quiz.explain: A waterfall shows the cumulative effect of sequential positive and negative values, which is exactly an opening to closing bridge. A funnel is for drop-off between ordered stages and a pie shows shares of a whole.

recap: Parameters rewrite the SQL (typed marker, default value, array_contains for multi-select, .min/.max for ranges, OR IS NULL for All) and always rerun the query. Field filters are the default for small data and cascade. Scope is global, page, or fixed widget-level, and widgets can ignore filters. Match the chart to the question: line trend, bar compare, pie share, histogram spread, scatter/bubble relation, funnel drop-off, waterfall bridge, counter KPI.

title: Sharing and Embedding Dashboards, Scheduled Refresh and SQL Alerts

concepts.heading: Publish Settings and Access Levels
concepts.body: Sharing starts with Publish, where you choose whose data permissions the queries use. Share data permissions (the default) runs queries as the publisher, so viewers need no access to the underlying data, which fits managers who must not touch the tables, but it can expose data they have not been granted. Individual data permissions runs queries as each viewer, so Unity Catalog row filters and column masks apply per person; compute still comes from the publisher. Access levels are CAN VIEW and CAN RUN to look and interact, CAN EDIT to edit and publish, and CAN MANAGE to change permissions and delete. A registered account member without workspace access is capped at CAN RUN, even if the dialog shows more. Share with a user, a group, or everyone in the account with Anyone in my account can view. Dashboards also inherit the permissions of the folder that holds them. A draft always uses the viewer's own data permissions, whatever the published setting is.

concepts.heading: Embedding a Dashboard
concepts.body: Only published dashboards can be embedded. Basic embedding generates iframe code from the Share dialog; viewers sign in with their Databricks account, only users granted access can see it, and a workspace admin must first define the allowed embedding surfaces. When the viewers are customers or partners who have no Databricks account, use embedding for external users, in which your application authenticates with a service principal and an OAuth token, and the user never signs in to Databricks. Databricks recommends publishing such a dashboard with individual data permissions and giving the service principal only the access it needs, because with shared data permissions the publisher's access determines the data. If an iframe stays blank, check in order: the dashboard is published, the viewer has access, the admin allowed the surface, and the browser accepts third-party cookies. Embedded viewers can refresh the dashboard on demand.

concepts.heading: Scheduled Refresh and Subscriptions
concepts.body: A schedule runs all the dataset SQL at a chosen frequency, start time and time zone, and fills the query result cache so the first viewer after the run opens the dashboard quickly. With shared data permissions the cache is shared by all viewers, so one early run helps the Monday crowd. The dashboard cache is best effort and can serve results up to a day old, and a pipeline finishing does not refresh it, so a schedule is the reliable way. With individual data permissions each viewer keeps a personal cache; a viewer chooses Refresh data for me to warm it without notifications, or Refresh data for me & email to also get a snapshot, or Inactive for me to opt out. A start time anchors the cadence: every 4 hours from 15:10 runs at 15:10, 19:10 and 23:10 and resets to 15:10 the next day. Subscriptions send PDF or image snapshots to email, Slack or Microsoft Teams, with optional CSV, TSV or Excel data.

concepts.heading: Databricks SQL Alerts
concepts.body: An alert runs a query on a schedule and notifies people when a condition on the result is met. In the alert editor you write the query, pick a SQL warehouse, set a schedule, choose the condition and the notification recipients. The condition checks the first value of a column or an aggregate such as sum or average, compares it with a static value using an operator, and Test condition previews it. Current alerts own their query: you cannot pick an existing saved query, so paste the SQL in. Each evaluation ends as OK, TRIGGERED or ERROR, and a recovered metric returns to OK. By default you are notified when the alert triggers. A notification frequency repeats the message until the alert returns to OK, Notify on OK sends a message when the alert returns to OK, and Empty result state decides the status when the query returns no rows. Recipients can be users or notification destinations that a workspace admin defined, such as a webhook.

examPoints: A question about viewers with no access to the tables is testing Share data permissions, while one about per-person row filters or masks is testing Individual data permissions.

A question about customers outside the account seeing a dashboard in a portal is testing embedding for external users with a service principal and OAuth, and a blank iframe is testing publish, access, allowed surfaces and cookies.

A question about slow first loads or fresh personal results is testing a schedule that fills the cache and Refresh data for me; one about repeated or recovery messages is testing notification frequency and Notify on OK.

quiz.q: A support lead receives one alert email when the open ticket count passes a limit, but she wants the email repeated until the count is back under the limit. Where is this configured?
choices: In the dashboard schedule dialog, by adding a second subscriber who receives the failure snapshot as well
In the advanced settings, through Empty result state, which keeps the alert triggered until the query returns rows again
In the alert condition, by lowering the threshold so the alert keeps evaluating as triggered each time
In the alert's Notifications, with a repeat frequency until OK
quiz.explain: The notification frequency repeats messages until the alert returns to OK. Notify on OK is the separate setting that sends a message at recovery, and Empty result state only chooses the status for a query with no rows.

quiz.q: A company wants customers, who are not members of its Databricks account, to see a dashboard inside the company's own web portal. Which approach fits?
choices: Embedding for external users, where the application authenticates with a service principal and OAuth
Basic embedding, after adding every customer to the Databricks account as a registered member
A shareable link with Anyone in my account can view, pasted into the portal as a normal hyperlink
A scheduled subscription that emails each customer a PDF of the dashboard after every refresh run
quiz.explain: Embedding for external users lets an application show a dashboard to people without Databricks accounts by authenticating as a service principal. Basic embedding and account-level links require each viewer to be a known account member.

recap: Publish chooses whose data permissions run the queries: shared for viewers without data access, individual for row filters and masks per person. CAN RUN/VIEW use, CAN EDIT edit and publish, CAN MANAGE permissions and delete. Embed only published dashboards: basic with sign-in, external users with a service principal. A schedule fills the cache (shared or personal) and drives subscriptions. Alerts own their query; use frequency to repeat and Notify on OK for recovery.

title: AI/BI Genie Agents: Purpose, Components and Creating a Genie Agent

concepts.heading: What Genie Agents Are For
concepts.body: Genie lets business users ask questions of governed data in plain language and get a table, a generated SQL query and sometimes a chart. The family has three parts. Genie One is the simple interface where business users discover and chat with data. Genie Agents (formerly Genie spaces) are the domain-specific environments where data teams set up trusted data, metrics and rules that power the answers. Genie Code is the coding and data assistant for technical users in the workspace (notebooks, pipelines, dashboards and more), and it was formerly called Databricks Assistant. An AI/BI dashboard is a fixed set of questions the analyst chose in advance, while an agent answers new questions inside the boundaries the analyst configured. Everything stays under Unity Catalog governance, so an agent is a curated natural-language front end, not a bypass around permissions. Genie is nondeterministic like other language models, so the setup work is what makes answers consistent.

concepts.heading: Requirements and Two Kinds of Credentials
concepts.body: The data of an agent must be in Unity Catalog, and an agent can include tables, views and metric views up to a documented maximum. Compute must be a pro or serverless SQL warehouse. To create or edit one, the author needs the Databricks SQL entitlement, CAN USE on the warehouse, and SELECT on the data. Saving a default warehouse embeds the author's compute credentials into the agent, so end users need no warehouse permission. Data access is different: it is always evaluated with the asking user's own Unity Catalog permissions, so two users asking the same question can get different rows when a row filter or a column mask applies, and queries are attributed to the asking user in query history. Sharing an agent therefore does not grant data. The creator automatically gets CAN MANAGE. When creating an agent, Genie Code launches and suggests table descriptions and example queries that the author reviews and accepts or rejects.

concepts.heading: Components That Give Genie Context
concepts.body: An agent writes SQL from the context it is given. The data comes first: attached tables, views and metric views, with Unity Catalog names and descriptions, and Genie queries only attached sources. Example SQL queries pair a question, titled the way users ask it, with the correct SQL. Parameterized examples and Unity Catalog SQL functions are trusted assets: when Genie uses one, the answer is marked as verified, and users need EXECUTE on a function. Text instructions hold general rules, such as the fiscal year start, and should be used last, after SQL examples and expressions. The knowledge store adds agent-level descriptions and synonyms, hidden columns, join relationships, and SQL expressions that define measures, filters and dimensions such as `orders.amount > 10000` called large orders. Prompt matching, format assistance and entity matching, helps map words to stored values such as Florida to FL. None of this changes the Unity Catalog metadata.

concepts.heading: Starting Small and Settings
concepts.body: Databricks advises starting as small as possible: a narrow purpose and audience, only the tables needed (about five or fewer is ideal), and few instructions, then iterating on real questions. If the source has many normalized tables, pre-join them into views or metric views and hide confusing or duplicate columns, because simpler data gives better SQL. Prefer SQL expressions and example SQL over free text, avoid instructions that contradict each other, and keep column descriptions in Unity Catalog accurate. In the agent settings you set the title, default warehouse, description, tags, thumbnail and common questions. Author-defined common (sample) questions appear first on the landing page, and Genie fills any remaining slots with generated ones. A domain expert, typically an analyst who knows the SQL and the business terms, should curate the agent rather than a general developer.

examPoints: A question about what an agent adds beyond a dashboard, or which product is for business users versus developers, is testing Genie One and Genie Agents for business questions and Genie Code for technical users.

A question about two users receiving different answers or a user who cannot see data is testing that warehouse access is embedded from the author while data access is the asking user's own Unity Catalog permission.
A question about inconsistent answers or business terms is testing example SQL, trusted assets, SQL expressions, synonyms and entity matching, and starting small with pre-joined views.

quiz.q: Users of a Genie Agent keep asking about "large orders", and the generated SQL applies a different threshold each time. The rule is simple: an order over a fixed amount is large. What is the best fix?
choices: Add a paragraph of text instructions explaining the threshold and ask the users to repeat the term in each question
Rename the amount column in Unity Catalog to large_order_amount so that the name carries the meaning
Define a filter SQL expression in the knowledge store, with the condition and the synonym large orders
Create an example query for every possible phrasing of the question and remove the other instructions
quiz.explain: Business terms that are simple conditions belong in a SQL expression of type filter, with synonyms. Text instructions are a last resort and are less reliable, and changing Unity Catalog names affects every consumer.

quiz.q: A regional manager has SELECT only on EMEA rows of a sales table through a row filter. A finance director has SELECT on all rows. Both ask the same question in the same Genie Agent. What happens?
choices: Each user's own Unity Catalog permissions decide the rows returned
Both users receive the finance director's result, because the agent runs with its author's data permissions only
The regional manager gets an error, since a row filter blocks every query that comes from any agent
Both users receive the EMEA rows only, because an agent applies the strictest permission of its users
quiz.explain: The author's embedded credentials only give warehouse access. Data access is always evaluated per asking user, so Unity Catalog row filters and column masks are enforced for each person.

recap: Genie One and Genie Agents serve business users; Genie Code serves technical users. An agent needs Unity Catalog data and a pro or serverless SQL warehouse; the author's embedded credentials give compute only, and data access is always the asking user's. Context = tables, example SQL, trusted assets (parameterized examples, SQL functions), SQL expressions, synonyms, prompt matching, then text instructions last. Start small, pre-join, hide confusing columns.

title: Genie Agents: Permissions, Distribution, Monitoring, Benchmarks and Refreshing Metadata

concepts.heading: Permissions on a Genie Agent
concepts.body: A Genie Agent has four permission levels. CAN VIEW and CAN RUN give the same abilities: see the agent, ask questions, give feedback. CAN EDIT adds adding and editing instructions, sample questions and included tables, and running benchmarks. CAN MANAGE adds monitoring, changing permissions, deleting the agent and viewing other users' conversations. A co-author who should tune the agent but not control sharing therefore gets CAN EDIT. Share with users or groups, including all account users, or place agents in a workspace folder, because agents are workspace objects that inherit the folder's permissions. To use an agent, a person also needs the consumer access or Databricks SQL entitlement and at least SELECT on every Unity Catalog object it uses. A user who opens a shared agent and gets no data is missing data permission, not agent permission. Reading other people's conversations needs CAN MANAGE and the conversation set to Reviewable by agent managers.

concepts.heading: Distributing an Agent
concepts.body: The simplest distribution is the shareable link: users who hold access open it directly. To show an agent inside an internal portal or website, an agent author with CAN MANAGE chooses Share and Embed space to copy iframe code. A workspace admin must have configured the allowed embedding surfaces first, and every end user still needs access to the agent and to the data; embedded users can ask questions but not edit the agent. Add `allow="clipboard-write"` to the iframe so users can copy results and links. For a backend service that asks questions without a person at a browser, use the Genie Conversation API with a service principal authenticated through OAuth M2M, with CAN VIEW on the agent and SELECT on the data; where a user sits at a browser, OAuth for users is the production choice. Agents can be certified or marked deprecated so that people find the trusted ones.

concepts.heading: Monitoring and Feedback
concepts.body: Each answer asks the user Is this correct? Yes confirms, Fix it flags a wrong answer and may regenerate it, and Request review sends it to the agent's managers. This feedback never changes the agent by itself; it shows editors where to add an example query, a SQL expression or an instruction. The Monitor tab lists every question and answer and can be filtered by time, rating, user and status. The weekly digest shows message volume, active users and feedback, and Analyze Agent Usage asks Genie Code to summarize common topics and recurring issues from recent messages. When Genie answers wrongly, an editor opens Show code, corrects and runs the SQL, then uses Add as instruction so the fixed query becomes an example for similar questions, or Add as benchmark to keep it as a test. Monitoring is part of the job because data and questions keep changing.

concepts.heading: Benchmarks and Refreshing Prompt Matching
concepts.body: Benchmarks are a saved set of test questions you run to measure accuracy after each change. In Chat mode a benchmark question should carry a SQL Answer, a query whose result is the correct answer, because only those questions are scored automatically; the others need manual review. Genie rates a response Good when its result set matches the SQL Answer, even if rows are sorted differently, and Bad when it errors, returns nothing, adds extra columns or gives a different single value. Users phrase the same need in many ways, so add two to four phrasings per common question, all pointing to the same SQL Answer. Benchmarks run as fresh conversations using the agent's instructions, and Genie Code can review a whole run for improvements. Entity matching keeps a stored list of a column's distinct values; when new values or formats arrive, use Refresh prompt matching on the column so Florida still maps to the new codes.

examPoints: A question about a colleague who may tune instructions but not change sharing is testing CAN EDIT versus CAN MANAGE, and one about reading other users' conversations is testing CAN MANAGE with Reviewable by agent managers.
A question about a portal, an iframe or a scheduled service is testing Embed space with allowed surfaces and CAN MANAGE, or a service principal with OAuth M2M, CAN VIEW and SELECT.

A question about benchmark accuracy not shown, extra columns, phrasing variants, or stale value lists is testing SQL Answer, Good versus Bad ratings, two to four phrasings, and Refresh prompt matching.

quiz.q: Users of a Genie Agent click Fix it on many answers about fiscal quarters and add comments. The analyst expects the agent to behave better next week without any change. What is true?
choices: The agent retrains nightly on the comments, so fiscal quarters improve once about a week of feedback exists in Monitor
Feedback alone changes nothing; editors add instructions or examples from it
Each Fix it click creates an instruction, but only a user with CAN MANAGE can switch those instructions on for everyone
Fix it rewrites the Unity Catalog column descriptions, which Genie then reads on the next question it answers
quiz.explain: Genie's behavior does not change from user feedback alone. Editors use feedback and the Monitor tab to find gaps, then add example SQL, SQL expressions or instructions, or fix the generated SQL and save it with Add as instruction.

quiz.q: An analyst adds benchmark questions to a Genie Agent but leaves the SQL Answer empty for most. After a Chat mode run, accuracy is missing for most questions. Why?
choices: Benchmarks need a CAN MANAGE user to approve each question before accuracy can be calculated
Entity matching must be enabled on every column before a benchmark run can compare result sets
Questions with several phrasings are skipped, so each must be merged into one canonical wording first
Only questions with a SQL Answer are scored automatically, and the others wait for manual review
quiz.explain: In Chat mode, Genie compares its result with the SQL Answer. Without one, nothing can be compared automatically, so the question needs manual review before it counts toward accuracy.

recap: CAN VIEW/RUN ask, CAN EDIT tunes, CAN MANAGE monitors, shares, deletes and reads conversations; users still need entitlement and SELECT. Share by link, folder, or Embed space (admin surfaces, CAN MANAGE); headless clients use a service principal with OAuth M2M. Feedback informs editors but changes nothing alone. Benchmarks need SQL Answers, use two to four phrasings, and Refresh prompt matching keeps entity values current.
